lines.text: Chit-thee. Ask old letters a question.
Ask a chatbot about a historical figure, and it will happily invent a quote.
Chit-thee answers only in the letters' own words.
Here, we ask Nehru directly, in say-ahns mode.
He answers in the first person,
and every underlined quote was found, word for word, in his letters.
Each citation points to a passage,
and opens the original 1929 scan.
Each page becomes text: from the PDF itself, from Gemma's vision, or from Tesseract.
Search blends keywords with Embedding Gemma vectors.
Gemma 4 writes the answer, as an archivist, or in the writer's own voice.
And every quote is checked against the page it cites. No evidence, no answer.
For Hindi, the O C R is chosen per page, and measured.
Gemma reads the vowel signs, but drops sentences and swaps in words. Tesseract, corrected by the PDF's own text, gets just half a percent wrong.
Now, archivist mode, answering in Hindi.
These are the same letters, in Premchand's 1931 translation.
Quotes are still checked, word for word,
and citations work in every script,
down to the Hindi page scan.
Nothing leaves this laptop. Gemma 4 and Embedding Gemma run locally, through Oh-lama. Family letters stay with the family.
Chit-thee. Let the letters speak for themselves.
